statement: Show that $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\,dx=\frac{\pi}{4}$, and interpret the result geometrically.
solution: Substitute $x=\sin\theta$, $dx=\cos\theta\,d\theta$; when $x=0,\theta=0$ and $x=1,\theta=\pi/2$. Then $\int_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1-x^{2}}dx=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\cos^{2}\theta\,d\theta =\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\tfrac{1+\cos2\theta}{2}d\theta=\left[\tfrac{\theta}{2}+\tfrac{\sin2\theta}{4}\right]_{0}^{\pi/2}=\tfrac{\pi}{4}$. Geometrically this is the area of a quarter of the unit circle, $\pi/4$.
hints: Use $x=\sin\theta$ to remove the square root.
Recognise the region as a quarter unit circle.
